solution:
[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives the third term as \(-\frac{8}{3}x^{3/2}\); expanding \((x-2)^2\sqrt{x}\) and integrating gives \(+\frac{8}{3}x^{3/2}\). The answer below is correct.]

Expand the square and integrate term by term (power rule).
\(\int(x-2)^2\sqrt{x}\,dx=\int(x^2-4x+4)\,x^{1/2}\,dx=\int\left(x^{5/2}-4x^{3/2}+4x^{1/2}\right)dx\)
\(=\dfrac{2}{7}x^{7/2}-\dfrac{8}{5}x^{5/2}+\dfrac{8}{3}x^{3/2}+c\)

Divide \(x^7\) by \(x+1\); since \(x^7=(x+1)(x^6-x^5+x^4-x^3+x^2-x+1)-1\),
\(\dfrac{x^7}{x+1}=x^6-x^5+x^4-x^3+x^2-x+1-\dfrac{1}{x+1}\).
Integrating each term:
\(\int\dfrac{x^7}{x+1}\,dx=\dfrac{x^7}{7}-\dfrac{x^6}{6}+\dfrac{x^5}{5}-\dfrac{x^4}{4}+\dfrac{x^3}{3}-\dfrac{x^2}{2}+x-\log|x+1|+c\)

Substitution. Put \(u=t+1\), so \(t=u-1,\ dt=du\) and \(t^3=(u-1)^3=u^3-3u^2+3u-1\).
\(\int\dfrac{t^3}{(t+1)^2}\,dt=\int\dfrac{u^3-3u^2+3u-1}{u^2}\,du=\int\left(u-3+\dfrac{3}{u}-\dfrac{1}{u^2}\right)du\)
\(=\dfrac{u^2}{2}-3u+3\log|u|+\dfrac{1}{u}\).
Re-substituting \(u=t+1\):
\(=\dfrac{(t+1)^2}{2}-3(t+1)+3\log|t+1|+\dfrac{1}{t+1}+c\)

Split the fraction using \(\dfrac{1}{\cos^2x}=\sec^2x\) and \(\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos^2x}=\sec x\tan x\).
\(\int\dfrac{3-2\sin x}{\cos^2x}\,dx=3\int\sec^2x\,dx-2\int\sec x\tan x\,dx\)
\(=3\tan x-2\sec x+c\)

Use \(\sin^6\theta+\cos^6\theta=1-3\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta\), so the integrand becomes
\(\dfrac{1-3\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta}{\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta}=\dfrac{1}{\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta}-3=\sec^2\theta+\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta-3\)
(since \(\dfrac{1}{\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta}=\dfrac{\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta}{\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta}\)).
\(\int\left(\sec^2\theta+\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta-3\right)d\theta=\tan\theta-\cot\theta-3\theta+c\)

Convert the product to a sum. First \(\cos 3x\cos x=\tfrac12(\cos 4x+\cos 2x)\), so
\(\cos 3x\cos 2x\cos x=\tfrac12\cos 2x(\cos 4x+\cos 2x)=\tfrac14(\cos 6x+\cos 2x+\cos 4x+1)\).
\(\int\cos 3x\cos 2x\cos x\,dx=\dfrac14\left(\dfrac{\sin 6x}{6}+\dfrac{\sin 2x}{2}+\dfrac{\sin 4x}{4}+x\right)\)
\(=\dfrac{x}{4}+\dfrac{\sin 2x}{8}+\dfrac{\sin 4x}{16}+\dfrac{\sin 6x}{24}+c\)

Simplify the fraction first. By factor formulae \(\cos 7x-\cos 8x=2\sin\tfrac{15x}{2}\sin\tfrac{x}{2}\), and multiplying \(1+2\cos 5x\) by \(2\sin\tfrac{5x}{2}\) gives \(2\sin\tfrac{15x}{2}\), so \(1+2\cos 5x=\dfrac{\sin(15x/2)}{\sin(5x/2)}\).
Hence \(\dfrac{\cos 7x-\cos 8x}{1+2\cos 5x}=2\sin\tfrac{x}{2}\sin\tfrac{5x}{2}=\cos 2x-\cos 3x\).
\(\int(\cos 2x-\cos 3x)\,dx=\dfrac{\sin 2x}{2}-\dfrac{\sin 3x}{3}+c\)

Simplify the argument with half-angles:
\(\dfrac{1+\sin x}{\cos x}=\dfrac{\left(\cos\frac{x}{2}+\sin\frac{x}{2}\right)^2}{\cos^2\frac{x}{2}-\sin^2\frac{x}{2}}=\dfrac{1+\tan\frac{x}{2}}{1-\tan\frac{x}{2}}=\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}+\dfrac{x}{2}\right)\).
So \(\cot^{-1}\left(\tan\left(\tfrac{\pi}{4}+\tfrac{x}{2}\right)\right)=\cot^{-1}\left(\cot\left(\tfrac{\pi}{4}-\tfrac{x}{2}\right)\right)=\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\dfrac{x}{2}\).
\(\int\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\dfrac{x}{2}\right)dx=\dfrac{\pi x}{4}-\dfrac{x^2}{4}+c\)

Substitution. Put \(t=1+\log x\), so \(dt=\dfrac{1}{x}\,dx\).
\(\int\dfrac{(1+\log x)^3}{x}\,dx=\int t^3\,dt=\dfrac{t^4}{4}=\dfrac{(1+\log x)^4}{4}+c\)

Express the inverse-cot as a difference of arctangents. Since \(\dfrac{x-(x-1)}{1+x(x-1)}=\dfrac{1}{1-x+x^2}\),
\(\cot^{-1}(1-x+x^2)=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{1}{1-x+x^2}=\tan^{-1}x-\tan^{-1}(x-1)\).
Integrate each by parts, using \(\int\tan^{-1}u\,du=u\tan^{-1}u-\tfrac12\log(1+u^2)\):
\(\int\cot^{-1}(1-x+x^2)\,dx=x\tan^{-1}x-\dfrac12\log(1+x^2)-(x-1)\tan^{-1}(x-1)+\dfrac12\log\!\left(1+(x-1)^2\right)+c\)

Substitution. Put \(t=\log x\), so \(dt=\dfrac{1}{x}\,dx\).
\(\int\dfrac{1}{x\sin^2(\log x)}\,dx=\int\operatorname{cosec}^2t\,dt=-\cot t=-\cot(\log x)+c\)

Substitution. Put \(t=x^{3/2}\), so \(dt=\tfrac{3}{2}x^{1/2}\,dx\), i.e. \(\sqrt{x}\,dx=\tfrac{2}{3}\,dt\).
\(\int\sqrt{x}\,\sec\!\left(x^{3/2}\right)\tan\!\left(x^{3/2}\right)dx=\dfrac{2}{3}\int\sec t\tan t\,dt=\dfrac{2}{3}\sec t=\dfrac{2}{3}\sec\!\left(x^{3/2}\right)+c\)

Use \(1+\cos x=2\cos^2\tfrac{x}{2}\), so \(\log(1+\cos x)=\log 2+2\log\left|\cos\tfrac{x}{2}\right|\). For the second term, integrate by parts with \(\int\tan\tfrac{x}{2}\,dx=-2\log\left|\cos\tfrac{x}{2}\right|\):
\(\int x\tan\tfrac{x}{2}\,dx=-2x\log\left|\cos\tfrac{x}{2}\right|+2\int\log\left|\cos\tfrac{x}{2}\right|dx\).
Subtracting, the remaining integral terms cancel:
\(\int\left[\log(1+\cos x)-x\tan\tfrac{x}{2}\right]dx=x\log 2+2x\log\left|\cos\tfrac{x}{2}\right|=x\log(1+\cos x)+c\)

Substitution. Put \(t=x^3\), so \(dt=3x^2\,dx\).
\(\int\dfrac{x^2}{\sqrt{1-x^6}}\,dx=\dfrac{1}{3}\int\dfrac{dt}{\sqrt{1-t^2}}=\dfrac{1}{3}\sin^{-1}t=\dfrac{1}{3}\sin^{-1}\!\left(x^3\right)+c\)

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives \(\frac{1}{4}\log|3-2\cot x|\), having wrongly simplified \(\cot 2x\) to \(2\cot x\); the correct answer is \(\frac{1}{4}\log|3-\cot 2x|\). The answer below is correct.]

Use \(1-\cos 4x=2\sin^2 2x\), so the integrand is \(\dfrac{1}{2\sin^2 2x\,(3-\cot 2x)}\). Put \(t=\cot 2x\), so \(dt=-2\operatorname{cosec}^2 2x\,dx\), i.e. \(\dfrac{dx}{\sin^2 2x}=-\dfrac{dt}{2}\).
\(\int\dfrac{dx}{(1-\cos 4x)(3-\cot 2x)}=-\dfrac{1}{4}\int\dfrac{dt}{3-t}=\dfrac{1}{4}\log|3-t|=\dfrac{1}{4}\log|3-\cot 2x|+c\)

Integrate by parts and use a cancelling pair. \(\int\log(\log x)\,dx=x\log(\log x)-\int\dfrac{dx}{\log x}\). Also \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\dfrac{x}{\log x}=\dfrac{1}{\log x}-\dfrac{1}{(\log x)^2}\), so \(\int\dfrac{dx}{(\log x)^2}=\int\dfrac{dx}{\log x}-\dfrac{x}{\log x}\).
Adding, the \(\int\dfrac{dx}{\log x}\) terms cancel:
\(\int\left[\log(\log x)+\dfrac{1}{(\log x)^2}\right]dx=x\log(\log x)-\dfrac{x}{\log x}+c\)

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives an inverse-tangent form, but the Weierstrass denominator \(2\cos x+3\sin x\) has real roots, so the antiderivative is logarithmic, not \(\tan^{-1}\). The correct answer is \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}\log\left|\tan\frac{x+\varphi}{2}\right|+c\), \(\varphi=\tan^{-1}\frac{2}{3}\). The answer below is correct.]

Denominator of the form \(a\cos x+b\sin x\). Write \(2\cos x+3\sin x=\sqrt{13}\,\sin(x+\varphi)\) with \(\cos\varphi=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}},\ \sin\varphi=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\), i.e. \(\varphi=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{2}{3}\).
\(\int\dfrac{dx}{2\cos x+3\sin x}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{13}}\int\operatorname{cosec}(x+\varphi)\,dx=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{13}}\log\left|\tan\dfrac{x+\varphi}{2}\right|+c,\quad\varphi=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{2}{3}\)

Trigonometric substitution. Put \(x=\sec\theta\), so \(dx=\sec\theta\tan\theta\,d\theta\) and \(\sqrt{x^2-1}=\tan\theta\).
\(\int\dfrac{dx}{x^3\sqrt{x^2-1}}=\int\dfrac{\sec\theta\tan\theta}{\sec^3\theta\tan\theta}\,d\theta=\int\cos^2\theta\,d\theta=\dfrac{\theta}{2}+\dfrac{\sin\theta\cos\theta}{2}\).
With \(\theta=\sec^{-1}x,\ \cos\theta=\dfrac{1}{x},\ \sin\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt{x^2-1}}{x}\):
\(=\dfrac{1}{2}\sec^{-1}x+\dfrac{\sqrt{x^2-1}}{2x^2}+c\)

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key's \(\sin^{-1}\) argument is \(\frac{2x-1}{\sqrt{7}}\); completing the square on \(-2x^2+x+3\) gives the argument \(\frac{4x-1}{5}\). The answer below is correct.]

Linear over \(\sqrt{\text{quadratic}}\). Write \(3x+1=-\tfrac{3}{4}(-4x+1)+\tfrac{7}{4}\), where \(-4x+1=\dfrac{d}{dx}(-2x^2+x+3)\).
First part: \(-\tfrac{3}{4}\int\dfrac{-4x+1}{\sqrt{-2x^2+x+3}}\,dx=-\tfrac{3}{4}\cdot 2\sqrt{-2x^2+x+3}=-\tfrac{3}{2}\sqrt{-2x^2+x+3}\).
Second part, complete the square \(-2x^2+x+3=2\left[\dfrac{25}{16}-\left(x-\tfrac{1}{4}\right)^2\right]\):
\(\tfrac{7}{4}\int\dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{-2x^2+x+3}}=\dfrac{7}{4\sqrt{2}}\sin^{-1}\dfrac{4x-1}{5}\).
\(\therefore\ \int\dfrac{3x+1}{\sqrt{-2x^2+x+3}}\,dx=-\dfrac{3}{2}\sqrt{-2x^2+x+3}+\dfrac{7}{4\sqrt{2}}\sin^{-1}\dfrac{4x-1}{5}+c\)

Integration by parts with \(u=\log(x^2+1),\ dv=dx\).
\(\int\log(x^2+1)\,dx=x\log(x^2+1)-\int\dfrac{2x^2}{x^2+1}\,dx=x\log(x^2+1)-2\int\left(1-\dfrac{1}{x^2+1}\right)dx\)
\(=x\log(x^2+1)-2x+2\tan^{-1}x+c\)

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key has the factor \(\frac{1}{4}\), giving exactly twice the integrand on differentiation; the \(\frac{1}{2}\) from \(\sin x\cos x=\frac{1}{2}\sin 2x\) was dropped, so the correct factor is \(\frac{1}{8}\). The answer below is correct.]

First \(\sin x\cos x=\tfrac12\sin 2x\), so the integral is \(\tfrac12\int e^{2x}\sin 2x\,dx\). Using \(\int e^{ax}\sin bx\,dx=\dfrac{e^{ax}(a\sin bx-b\cos bx)}{a^2+b^2}\) with \(a=b=2\):
\(\tfrac12\int e^{2x}\sin 2x\,dx=\tfrac12\cdot\dfrac{e^{2x}(2\sin 2x-2\cos 2x)}{8}=\dfrac{e^{2x}(\sin 2x-\cos 2x)}{8}+c\)

Partial fractions: \(\dfrac{x^2}{(x-1)(3x-1)(3x-2)}=\dfrac{A}{x-1}+\dfrac{B}{3x-1}+\dfrac{C}{3x-2}\). By the cover-up rule, \(A=\tfrac12,\ B=\tfrac16,\ C=-\tfrac43\).
\(\int=\dfrac12\log|x-1|+\dfrac16\cdot\dfrac13\log|3x-1|-\dfrac43\cdot\dfrac13\log|3x-2|\)
\(=\dfrac12\log|x-1|+\dfrac{1}{18}\log|3x-1|-\dfrac{4}{9}\log|3x-2|+c\)

Write \(\sin x+\sin 2x=\sin x(1+2\cos x)\) and multiply numerator and denominator by \(\sin x\). With \(t=\cos x,\ dt=-\sin x\,dx\):
\(\int\dfrac{dx}{\sin x(1+2\cos x)}=-\int\dfrac{dt}{(1-t^2)(1+2t)}=-\int\dfrac{dt}{(1-t)(1+t)(1+2t)}\).
Partial fractions give \(\dfrac{1/6}{1-t}-\dfrac{1/2}{1+t}+\dfrac{4/3}{1+2t}\), so
\(=\dfrac16\log|1-\cos x|+\dfrac12\log|1+\cos x|-\dfrac23\log|1+2\cos x|+c\)

Put \(t=\tan x,\ dt=\sec^2x\,dx\); then complete the square \(7+2t-t^2=8-(t-1)^2\).
\(\int\sec^2x\sqrt{7+2\tan x-\tan^2x}\,dx=\int\sqrt{8-(t-1)^2}\,dt\).
Using \(\int\sqrt{a^2-u^2}\,du=\dfrac{u}{2}\sqrt{a^2-u^2}+\dfrac{a^2}{2}\sin^{-1}\dfrac{u}{a}\) with \(u=t-1,\ a=2\sqrt{2}\):
\(=\dfrac{\tan x-1}{2}\sqrt{7+2\tan x-\tan^2x}+4\sin^{-1}\dfrac{\tan x-1}{2\sqrt{2}}+c\)

Factor the denominator: \(x^3+3x^2-x-3=x^2(x+3)-(x+3)=(x+3)(x-1)(x+1)\). Partial fractions:
\(\dfrac{x+5}{(x+3)(x-1)(x+1)}=\dfrac{1/4}{x+3}+\dfrac{3/4}{x-1}-\dfrac{1}{x+1}\).
\(\int\dfrac{x+5}{x^3+3x^2-x-3}\,dx=\dfrac14\log|x+3|+\dfrac34\log|x-1|-\log|x+1|+c\)

Multiply numerator and denominator by \(x^4\): \(\dfrac{1}{x(x^5+1)}=\dfrac{x^4}{x^5(x^5+1)}\). Put \(t=x^5,\ dt=5x^4\,dx\).
\(\int\dfrac{x^4}{x^5(x^5+1)}\,dx=\dfrac15\int\dfrac{dt}{t(t+1)}=\dfrac15\int\left(\dfrac1t-\dfrac{1}{t+1}\right)dt=\dfrac15\log\left|\dfrac{t}{t+1}\right|\)
\(=\dfrac15\log\left|\dfrac{x^5}{x^5+1}\right|+c\)

Write \(\sin x\cos x=\tan x\cos^2x\), so the integrand is \(\dfrac{\sqrt{\tan x}}{\tan x\cos^2x}=\dfrac{\sec^2x}{\sqrt{\tan x}}\). Put \(t=\tan x,\ dt=\sec^2x\,dx\).
\(\int\dfrac{\sqrt{\tan x}}{\sin x\cos x}\,dx=\int t^{-1/2}\,dt=2\sqrt{t}=2\sqrt{\tan x}+c\)

Put \(t=\tan x,\ dt=\sec^2x\,dx\); then \(\sec^2x=1+t^2\) and \(\operatorname{cosec}^2x=\dfrac{1+t^2}{t^2}\), giving
\(\sec^4x\operatorname{cosec}^2x\,dx=\dfrac{(1+t^2)^2}{t^2}\,dt=\left(t^{-2}+2+t^2\right)dt\).
\(\int\sec^4x\operatorname{cosec}^2x\,dx=-\dfrac1t+2t+\dfrac{t^3}{3}=\dfrac{\tan^3x}{3}+2\tan x-\cot x+c\)
